title: The Definition of Lying and Deception

summaries.example: Maya tells her friend, “I finished my homework,” even though she believes she did not finish it. She says this to make her friend believe it is true. The traditional definition counts this as a lie. If her friend does not believe her, Maya has still lied; success is not required.
summaries.summary: Philosophers do not all agree on what lying means. A widely discussed traditional definition has four parts: a person makes a statement, believes the statement is false, directs it to another person, and intends that person to believe it is true. Each part can be questioned. For example, a statement can accidentally be true even though the speaker thought it was false. A person may also use an ironic sentence, joke, or performance in an attempt to mislead. Some philosophers count these as lies, while others require an assertion or an act that invites trust. The source also separates lying from deception. Deception can involve making someone believe something false through words, actions, appearances, silence, or even a truthful statement. Some accounts include keeping a false belief in place or preventing someone from learning the truth; other accounts call that ignorance rather than deception. The entry studies these meanings rather than deciding the separate moral question of whether lying is always wrong.
key_ideas: The traditional definition says that lying involves making a statement one believes is false, to another person, with an aim of making that person believe it is true.
A statement can be a lie even when it turns out to be true, and even when the listener does not believe it.
The traditional definition usually does not count simply staying silent as lying, unless the silence is an agreed signal with a meaning.
Philosophers disagree about whether lying must involve an intention to deceive, an assertion, trust, or a statement that is actually false.
Deception is wider than lying: a person can deceive through actions, appearances, silence, or a truthful statement that leads someone to a false belief.
summaries.why_it_matters: Knowing what a word means helps us discuss real situations fairly. People may agree that someone caused confusion but disagree about whether the person lied, deceived, misled, or simply stayed silent. Careful definitions show which details matter: what was communicated, what the speaker believed, who was addressed, and what the speaker intended.

important_terms.definition: A sentence, sign, gesture, or other agreed-upon message that communicates an idea. Words, sign language, and Morse code can all be used to make statements.
The traditional idea that a lie says something the speaker believes is not true. The statement might accidentally turn out to be true.
The person or group being spoken to. A lie is usually understood as being directed at someone the speaker thinks can understand the message.
Trying to make the addressee believe that an untruthful statement is true. Some philosophers think this is required for lying; others disagree.
Making someone believe something false. Deception can happen through words, silence, actions, or appearances, and it may involve a statement that is actually true.

questions_to_think_about: If someone says something false as part of a joke, is it a lie if nobody is meant to believe it?
If a person tells the truth but carefully leaves out an important fact, are they lying, deceiving, or neither?
Should a lie still count if nobody believes it?
Can a person lie by using a special hand signal instead of words?

summaries.example: Suppose Lina tells Omar, “The report is finished,” while believing it is unfinished. She wants Omar to accept the proposition as true, but Omar already knows the report is incomplete and rejects her statement. On the traditional account, Lina has lied even though the report is not actually finished and Omar is not deceived. Now change the case: Lina truthfully says, “I submitted a draft,” while intending Omar to infer that she submitted the final report. This may be deception or paltering, but it is not a lie on the traditional account because she did not make a statement she believed to be false.
summaries.summary: The entry examines conceptual questions about lying and deception rather than settling their moral status. Its traditional account defines lying through four necessary conditions: making a statement, believing that statement to be untruthful, directing it to another person, and intending that person to believe the statement true. The conditions are independent. A statement need not be false in reality, and the lie need not persuade its audience. The account also distinguishes a statement from an assertion, so its treatment of irony, jokes, fiction, and acting can be broader than accounts that require an assertion or an invitation to trust. Critics challenge every part of the traditional account. They argue that omission, truthful but misleading statements, third-party listeners, coercive speech, or the absence of deceptive intention may still involve lying. Other critics add requirements, such as actual falsity, an intention to misrepresent the speaker’s belief, assertion, or a breach of trust. These disagreements generate deceptionist and non-deceptionist theories. The entry separately considers deception, which may involve false-belief formation or maintenance, loss of true belief, or blocked knowledge, depending on the theory. It may occur through language, action, appearance, silence, or truthful implications, and some accounts allow it to be unintentional.
key_ideas: The traditional definition, often represented as L1, requires a believed-false statement, an addressee, and an intention that the addressee believe the statement true.
L1 uses the speaker’s belief rather than actual falsity. Thus, a statement believed false can be true, and a statement believed true can be false without being a lie under L1.

An intention to deceive the particular addressee is stronger than merely intending that someone be deceived, or intending to misrepresent the speaker’s own beliefs. Several proposed definitions revise this point.

The definition of a statement does not automatically include assertion. Consequently, L1 can classify deceptive irony, jokes, fictional writing, or acting as lies if the required intention is present.

Deception is commonly treated as an achievement: it requires producing, preserving, or sometimes preventing a belief-related result. Accounts differ over whether unintentional deception and withholding truth count.

The major dispute divides deceptionists, who require deceptive intention, from non-deceptionists, who allow some non-deceptive lies, such as false statements made in a context where the speaker warrants their truth.
summaries.why_it_matters: The distinction between lying, deception, and misleading matters in ordinary judgment, law, communication, and trust. A person can communicate something untrue without asserting it, state something true while encouraging a false inference, or speak falsely without expecting belief. Philosophical definitions make these cases explicit instead of allowing one word to cover every kind of dishonesty.

important_terms.definition: A communicative act using conventional language or signs to express a proposition. It need not be an assertion: jokes, irony, fiction, and acting can still involve statements.
The traditional requirement that the speaker believes the proposition expressed is false or otherwise not true. It concerns the speaker’s belief, not necessarily the proposition’s actual truth.
The requirement that the untruthful statement be directed to another person whom the speaker regards as capable of understanding and forming beliefs from it.
The traditional requirement that the speaker aim for the addressee to believe the untruthful proposition is true. The lie need not succeed.
A communicative act that presents content as worthy of acceptance, often by inviting the hearer to rely on the speaker’s sincerity or trustworthiness.
A statement that is true but is used to produce a false belief or implication. It is often treated as deception or misleading, rather than lying, under the traditional definition.
The view that lying requires an intention to deceive. Simple versions require an untruthful statement and deceptive intention; more complex versions add assertion or a breach of trust.
The view that an intention to deceive is not necessary for lying. Some versions treat an untruthful assertion, or a statement made in a truth-warranting context, as sufficient.

questions_to_think_about: Does lying require intending a hearer to believe the proposition, or is intending to misrepresent the speaker’s belief enough?
Should an untruthful statement made under coercion count as an assertion and therefore as a lie?
Is a truthful statement that creates a false implication a lie, a deception, or merely misleading speech?
If a speaker knows the audience will reject a false statement, can the speaker still be lying?
Does preventing someone from learning a truth amount to deception, or only to keeping that person ignorant?

summaries.example: Jordan tells a coach, “I practiced every day,” while believing that this is false and hoping the coach will believe it. The coach is suspicious and does not believe Jordan. The traditional definition still calls Jordan’s act a lie because the attempt matters, not whether it works. But imagine Jordan says, “I practiced on Monday,” which is true, while leaving the coach with the false impression that Jordan practiced all week. Philosophers may call this misleading or paltering rather than lying.
summaries.summary: The philosophical problem is not simply whether a sentence is true or false. It is what makes an act a lie. The traditional definition says that a speaker makes a statement to another person, believes the statement is untruthful, and intends the other person to believe it is true. This account explains why a lie can fail to persuade and why a statement that turns out true can still be a lie. It also excludes many omissions, unless silence has been established as a meaningful signal. The entry presents objections to each condition. Some philosophers say lying can occur without a statement, with a truthful statement, toward an unintended listener, or without an intention to deceive. Others say the traditional definition is too broad and add actual falsity, assertion, or an intention to make the listener trust the speaker’s belief. These proposals form two broad camps. Deceptionists make deceptive intention necessary, while non-deceptionists argue that an untruthful assertion or a statement made in a context that warrants truth can be a lie even without that intention. Deception itself has a wider range in many theories: it can involve causing or preserving false belief, blocking true belief, or using words and behavior to create a mistaken impression. Whether such cases count as deception may depend on intention, evidence, and whether a belief was actually produced.
key_ideas: The traditional definition has four parts: statement, believed untruthfulness, an addressee, and an intention to make that addressee believe the statement.
Actual truth and believed truth can come apart. Someone may lie with a statement that happens to be true, or make a false statement without lying if they believe it is true.
On the traditional view, silence is not normally a lie because no statement was made, although an agreed silent signal can function as a statement.
Some philosophers think lying requires an assertion or a broken expectation of trust, which makes the category narrower than the traditional definition.
Deception can be broader than lying. It may use actions, appearances, silence, or true statements, and theories disagree about whether it must be intentional and successful.
The central disagreement is between deceptionists, who require deceptive intention, and non-deceptionists, who allow certain false assertions without that intention.
summaries.why_it_matters: These definitions help us notice why similar-looking cases may differ. A false statement, a lie, a misleading truth, an omission, and a mistaken explanation can have different structures. Clear distinctions are useful when people evaluate trust and responsibility, because they prevent us from assuming that every kind of misleading communication is exactly the same.

important_terms.definition: A message that uses agreed meanings, such as words, writing, sign language, or a special signal, to communicate an idea.
The idea that the speaker believes the statement is false or not true. This is different from the statement actually being false.
The person or people the speaker is addressing. A secret listener may not count as the addressee on some theories of lying.
A plan or aim to make another person accept something as true. The traditional view says this aim is part of lying.
A stronger kind of statement that presents information as something the listener should accept, often by relying on the speaker’s sincerity or trust.
Using a true statement to encourage someone to form a false belief or impression. Many philosophers distinguish this from lying.
A broad family of views saying that lying requires an intention to deceive. Some versions also require assertion or a broken trust relationship.
A family of views saying that lying does not always require an intention to deceive. Some require an untruthful assertion or a context where truth is being warranted.

questions_to_think_about: If a person uses a true fact to make a listener reach a false conclusion, what should we call the act?
Is a failed attempt to persuade still a lie? Why might success or failure matter?
Should a person be able to lie to someone who is secretly listening but is not being addressed?
What extra feature does an assertion have that a joke or an ironic remark might lack?
Can keeping someone from learning a fact be deception even when the person forms no false belief?
